scope.current_boundary: Analyse circular orbits in gravitational fields by relating gravitational force to the centripetal acceleration it causes; explain the conditions for a geostationary orbit.
scope.previous_boundary_used: Newton's law of gravitation for two point masses, including treating a uniform sphere as a point mass outside the sphere.
scope.next_boundary_checked: Derive the point-mass gravitational-field-strength equation from Newton's law and the definition of gravitational field strength. It is deliberately not taught here.

question_patterns_used.name: Quantitative calculation and multi-step derivation
question_patterns_used.lesson_response: Equating gravitational and centripetal force, deriving speed and period, then calculating an orbit radius.

question_patterns_used.name: Physical mechanism and field explanation
question_patterns_used.lesson_response: Explains that gravity is the inward centripetal force and why a perpendicular force does no work in a circular orbit.

question_patterns_used.name: Definition, law and conservation principle
question_patterns_used.lesson_response: Restates the controlled gravitation law and teaches all required geostationary conditions precisely.

questions_visited.why_selected: Directly requires equating gravitational and centripetal force to obtain orbital speed.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Show a symbolic derivation with a clear force-origin statement.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Set GMm/r^2 equal to mv^2/r and cancel satellite mass.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Treating centripetal force as a separate force or failing to use centre-to-centre radius.
lesson_sections_informed: Worked example: find an orbital speed

questions_visited.why_selected: Uses a body that remains above the same surface point and requires matching orbital period to rotational angular speed.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Connect angular speed, period and synchronous orbit.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: A body fixed above a surface point has the same period as the planet's rotation.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Assuming that an orbital period can be chosen independently of the surface rotation.

questions_visited.why_selected: Directly asks for geostationary orbit features.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: State precise orbital features rather than a vague description.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Recall period, direction and equatorial plane, then connect them to fixed surface position.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Giving only 24 hours and omitting direction or orbital plane.

questions_visited.why_selected: Tests whether fixed surface position is understood as an operational property of a geostationary satellite.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Compare a geostationary orbit with a polar orbit for communication.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Link fixed relative position to continuous communication coverage, while recognising orbit type matters.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Claiming every satellite remains fixed above one surface point.

questions_visited.why_selected: Tests the direction of gravitational force and its work in a circular orbit.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Explain why a radial force does no work on tangential displacement.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Gravity is radial while instantaneous displacement is tangential, so they are perpendicular.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Assuming every force that acts must change kinetic energy.
lesson_sections_informed: A common mistake: using altitude as r

questions_visited.why_selected: Asks for the origin of the centripetal force on an orbiting satellite.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Identify the physical force, not merely name centripetal force.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: The planet's gravitational attraction supplies the resultant inward force.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Naming a fictitious outward force or treating centripetal force as an extra interaction.

questions_visited.why_selected: Requires a satellite that remains above a planet surface point to have an orbital radius calculated from rotational period.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Use synchronous-period reasoning and circular-orbit relationships.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Use the planet rotation period as orbital period, then rearrange the circular-orbit relation for radius.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Using a height as radius or leaving days instead of SI seconds.
lesson_sections_informed: Worked example: estimate a geostationary orbit radius

questions_visited.why_selected: Uses a geostationary satellite over a 24-hour interval and reinforces a constant orbital position relative to Earth.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Recognise a quantity at the satellite remains constant during a circular geostationary orbit.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Orbital radius is constant, so the Earth-generated potential at the satellite is constant.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Assuming a changing time coordinate means the satellite's orbital radius changes.

definitions_considered.exact_text: gravitational force is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation
definitions_considered.reason: Previous lesson knowledge is explicitly required to relate gravity to centripetal acceleration.

definitions_considered.exact_text: gravitational force per unit mass acting on a small test mass
definitions_considered.reason: The next lesson derives the point-mass field-strength equation from this definition.

definitions_considered.exact_text: a region of space where a mass experiences a gravitational force
definitions_considered.reason: This term was taught in the preceding course module and is not a new formal-definition outcome here.

definitions_considered.exact_text: work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point
definitions_considered.reason: Gravitational potential is formally taught in course module 04; the selected question was used only for the fixed-radius idea.

formulas_considered.name: Newton's law of gravitation
conditions: Two point masses or points outside uniform spheres; r is centre-to-centre separation.
formulas_considered.reason: This is the gravitational-force expression that supplies centripetal force.

formulas_considered.name: Centripetal force
conditions: Uniform circular motion; F is the resultant inward force.
formulas_considered.reason: It is equated to gravitational force to analyse circular gravitational orbits.

formulas_considered.name: Centripetal acceleration
conditions: Uniform circular motion; acceleration is towards the centre.
formulas_considered.reason: The outcome explicitly requires relating gravity to centripetal acceleration; its meaning is explained while the force form is used algebraically.

formulas_considered.name: Newton's second law of motion
conditions: For constant mass, resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
formulas_considered.reason: Its constant-mass form explains why gravitational force causes centripetal acceleration, without adding a separate force.

formulas_considered.name: Gravitational field strength
conditions: Small test mass in a gravitational field.
formulas_considered.reason: Reserved for the immediately next lesson's derivation.

formulas_considered.name: Gravitational field strength due to a point mass
conditions: Point mass or position outside a uniform sphere.
formulas_considered.reason: It is the exact subject of the next lesson.

formulas_considered.name: Gravitational potential energy in a radial field
conditions: Point mass or outside a uniform sphere, with zero potential at infinity.
formulas_considered.reason: Potential and potential energy are reserved for course module 04.

formulas_considered.name: Gravitational potential due to a point mass
conditions: Point mass or outside a uniform sphere, with zero potential at infinity.
formulas_considered.reason: Potential is reserved for course module 04.

formulas_considered.name: Escape speed from gravitational field
conditions: Minimum speed to reach infinity with zero final speed.
formulas_considered.reason: Escape speed is a later gravitational-potential application.
